newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf shipping seen unruffled by U.S.-Iraq tension.
newsitem.headline: Gulf shipping seen unruffled by U.S.-Iraq tension.

text.p: A United States military build-up and tensions with Iraq pose little concern to shippers in the Gulf, one of the world's busiest waterways and conduit for much of the West's oil, industry officials said on Saturday.

They said risk premiums were unchanged since tensions between Washington and Baghdad rose last week, with the U.S. building up its military in the Gulf for possible wider strikes against Iraq and Baghdad's threats to shoot down U.S. planes.
Any military activity in the Gulf usually has a ripple effect on the oil, shipping and insurance markets.
Their unease usually centres on the strategic Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf, through which 15 million barrels of crude oil and refined products are shipped each day.
But industry officials said the latest tensions had not triggered concern among shippers in the Gulf, busy with up to 70 daily oil and cargo vessel movements.
Asked by Reuters to assess the danger for shipping in the northern Gulf, Mike Baxter, navigation coordinator for the independent Middle East Navigation Aids Service, said: "Zero".
"The whole area is monitored. The U.S. is here, the British, the French, the surrounding countries in the Gulf are all part of it. They all monitor because they all have a vested interest."
"It's business as usual. People outside the Gulf are over-reacting. The industry is not alarmed by the situation," said Nestor Mariano, a Gulf-based shipping insurance executive.

The United States sent Stealth and B-52 bombers to within striking distance of Iraq and is dispatching more troops and a second aircraft carrier to the region after Iraq threatened to target allied planes enforcing a no-fly zone in southern Iraq.
U.S., French and British naval vessels monitor shipping traffic in the Gulf as part of a multinational team enforcing a trade ban imposed on Baghdad after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Experts said on Friday that Iraq, which mined the Gulf during the 1990-91 Gulf crisis, had the capability of laying contact, magnetic and sound mines in the northern Gulf, despite the fact that its navy was destroyed in the 1991 Gulf War.

A senior Western officer told Reuters on Friday the Iraqi threat was minimal but that Iraq could still drop mines. "...You do not need warships. Pleasure boats or dhows (traditional wooden Gulf trading vessels) can do the job."
Industry officials said this was unlikely.
Asked to gauge the Iraqi potential to lay mines in the Gulf, Baxter told Reuters: "They may have the capabilities but they would not be able to implement it.

"Their whole area is monitored so closely, where perhaps troop movement and other installations on land are a little harder to identify, any movement offshore is so easy to identify, they just could not do it.
"For a pleasure craft to come outside the immediate limits of Iraq waters (would be) very noticeable," he said.
"I don't think it (the tension) will spill out of Iraq. It is not that easy for them (Iraqis) to move. How can they lay mines when they are not even allowed below" the no-fly zone, said Mariano.

The United States launched 44 missiles into southern Iraq after Iraq sent its troops into northern Iraq this month and widened a no-fly zone in the south. Iraq declared the zone void, but backed down on Friday on a pledge to shoot at Western planes patrolling its airspace.

"It's business as usual. There are no concerns at the moment. If insurance rates increase that would certainly alarm vessels," said a shipping executive in Saudi Arabia. "It would take an invasion of Kuwait or a ship to be sunk."
War premiums for ships had remained at 0.0275 percent of the cargo value since the latest tensions, Mariano said.
